chapters.summary: Council Member Rita Joseph introduces herself as Chair of the Committee on Higher Education and welcomes attendees to the joint hearing with the Committee on Education. She states the hearing topic is the use of the NYS Seal of Civic Readiness in DOE high schools and at CUNY.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph opens joint hearing on Seal of Civic Readiness

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Rita Joseph, Chair of the Committee on Higher Education.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Welcome to our joint hearing with the Committee on Education, chaired by Councilmember Eric Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Today's hearing is on the use of New York State's Seal of Civic Readiness in DOE's high school and at CUNY.

chapters.summary: Joseph lists Int 259 on dental care information, Res 418 on CUNY credit for the Seal, Res 451 on the Next Gen Civics Act, and proposed Res 620A on awarding the Seal in all NYC public high schools. She names the sponsors for each item.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph lists legislation before the committees

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Additionally,

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Our committees will hear the following legislation.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Intro 259, sponsored by Councilmember Shekhar Krishnan, amending the Administrative Code of the City of New York in relation to requiring the Department of Education to distribute information about the importance of dental care.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Reso 418, sponsored by Councilmember Dinowitz, calling on the City of University to ensure all campus award an appropriate number of college credits to students who earn New York State's Seal of Civic Readiness in high school.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Reso 451, sponsored by Councilmember Suzanne Joanne, calling on the New York State Legislature to pass and the Governor to sign.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Aid 9298 and a companion bill in the Senate which enact Next Gen Civics Act, providing hands-on project based on civic education to students in grades 9 through 12.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And proposed Reso 620A, also sponsored by Councilmember Dinowitz, calling on the New York City Department of Education to ensure that the New York State Seal of Civic Readiness is awarded in all New York City public high school to eligible students.

chapters.summary: Susan Zhuang says young New Yorkers are among the least civically engaged voters and that high-quality civic education increases voting and volunteering. She asks colleagues to support Res 451, which calls on the state to pass the Next Gen Civics Act for hands-on civics in grades 9-12.
chapters.title: Council Member Zhuang advocates for Res 451 and Next Gen Civics Act

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: First, let me ask Councilmember Zhuang to deliver her

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: marks on her bill.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you so much for two chairs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: As a mother of two, I deeply care about education of our city's children and knowing how important it is they be taught how to engage with government.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Right now, young people are not engaging

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Engaging in politics, young New Yorkers remain among the least civically engaged voters in the city.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Participating among schools in civic education reminds voluntary and uneven, but young people who receive high-quality civic education

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: are significantly more likely to vote, volunteer, and engage in their community as a result.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you to support Rizzo 451 calling on New York State Legislature to pass and the governor to sign A9298 and the companion bill in Senate, which would

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: enact the Next Gen Civic Act, providing hands-on projects based on civic education to students in grades 9 through 12.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: This instruction will include hands-on projects where students apply what they learn through activities like mock election, community projects, and policy simulations.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I encourage my colleagues to support this resolution and help our children learn about how our government

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: government to work in a way that will engage and excite them.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan

chapters.summary: Joseph says the Seal was implemented statewide in 2022 and recognizes proficiency in civic knowledge, skills, and action. She describes the point system, including social studies courses, Regents exams, research projects, service learning, and a civic capstone project.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph explains Seal of Civic Readiness requirements

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Krishnan.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Now for a little background on today's hearing topic, the Seal of Civic Readiness, which was implemented statewide in 2022, recognizes high school students who have attained a high level of proficiency.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: in civic knowledge, skills, and actions.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It also shows higher education institutions and employers that students have completed an action project in civics or social justice.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: To earn the seal of civic readiness, a student must earn points from a menu of various civic knowledge and participation benchmarks, which they

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: can select from, which in completing required advanced selective social studies high school courses, passing the social studies regents exam, carrying out a research project, completing a service

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: learning project of at least 25 hours, participating in extracurricular activity or work-based learning experiences of at least 40 hours,

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: and conducting a middle school or high school civic capstone project that addresses a real-world issue.

chapters.summary: Joseph says some NYC public high school graduates have come to CUNY with the Seal for several years. She says the committees want to explore how the Seal is promoted and encourage CUNY to accept it for credit or requirements to smooth the transition and improve timely graduation.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph outlines committee interest in CUNY credit and graduation

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Some New York City public high schools have graduated coming to CUNY with an earned SEAL civic readiness in their hands for several years now.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: At this hearing, the committees are interested in exploring how SEAL of civic readiness is being promoted and awarded across New York City public school high schools.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But the committee is also interested in encouraging CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: To accept the seal for college credit or in fulfillment of a common core or elective requirement.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I believe that that would help smooth the transition from high school to college for the DOE high school graduates who made the effort to earn the seal.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The committee further interested in whether awarding college credit for the seal of civic readiness would eventually improve students'chances of successfully

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: graduating from CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Our committees are also extremely interested in making sure CUNY students graduate in a timely manner so they can move on to pursue their careers as effectively and efficiently as possible.

chapters.summary: Eric Dinowitz introduces himself as Chair of the Committee on Education and as a NYC public schools and CUNY alum. He warns of deepening polarization and youth detachment from civics, and says the city must re-engage students in civic education.
chapters.title: Chair Dinowitz opens with personal background and polarization concerns

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Now let me turn it over to Chair Dinowitz for his opening remark on the hearing topic on his resolutions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Eric Dinowitz, Chair of the Committee on Education, but I think more importantly, New York City Public Schools alum and CUNY alum.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, we are in a time of deepening polarization, as was mentioned in Councilmember Krishnan's bill, misinformation or lies,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and people just becoming so detached from civics that it becomes critical that we do what we can in New York City to re-engage our youth, our kids in civic education

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and ensure those incentives are there for our schools to engage in that kind of education.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz reports that 8,000 students from 166 DOE high schools earned the Seal in 2024-2025, a 72% increase from the prior year. He notes only 643 seniors from 31 high schools earned it in the 2022 pilot year.
chapters.title: Dinowitz cites Seal growth statistics

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In the 2024-2025 school year, 8,000 students graduating from 166 DOE high schools earned the New York State Seal of Civic Readiness.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That was an impressive 72% increase from the previous year.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In June 2022, at the end of the state's pilot year, 643 graduating seniors from 31 high schools earned it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The numbers are climbing fast.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There's another reason this conversation matters.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: matters now.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says the State Board of Regents is moving to end specific Regents exam graduation requirements beginning with the class of 2028. He notes the Seal can currently replace the second social studies Regents exam but will no longer count toward a diploma under the state plan.
chapters.title: Dinowitz discusses Regents exam changes and Seal's diploma role

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Last month, the State Board of Regents authorized the State Ed Department to move forward with ending the requirement for students to pass specific set of Regents exams to graduate, beginning with the class of 2028.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Today, a student can use the seal of civic readiness in place of the second Regents social studies exam.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Under the state's plan, the seal will no longer count towards a diploma.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It would still be a recognition, but it's worth the students will depend on what colleges do with it.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says more than 60% of DOE graduates who go to college enroll at CUNY, so many incoming students likely have the Seal. He argues CUNY could award flexible Common Core or elective credits to help students meet requirements sooner.
chapters.title: Dinowitz notes CUNY enrollment and potential credit benefits

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: More than 60% of DUE graduates who go on to college enroll at CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So a substantial growing number of incoming CUNY students have likely earned the seal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If CUNY colleges awarded flexible Common Core or elective credits for it, those students could meet CUNY's general election requirements sooner.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says earning the Seal takes more than basics, including eight social studies credits and at least two civic participation points. He says the Seal should be recognized for the rigorous work students complete.
chapters.title: Dinowitz argues Seal rigor exceeds basics

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And earning a seal takes more than the basics.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Our last hearing was about Portrait of a Graduate, and there are some out there who are concerned about the rigor of our Regents exams.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But earning a seal takes more than the basics.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: To earn a Regents or Advanced Regents Diploma, every student must complete eight semester credits in social studies.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Four in global, two in U.S.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: History, one in econ, and one in participation in government.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The SEAL additionally requires at least two points in civic participation from things like service learning, civics projects, civic engagement, electives, extracurricular activities, or work-based learning.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz cites the NYC Campaign Finance Board that civic engagement course offerings vary by school funding and location. He notes only schools that apply to DOE can award the Seal, so a student's chance depends on which high school they attend.
chapters.title: Dinowitz cites CFB on unequal civic course access

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And according to the New York City Campaign Finance Board,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The number and diversity of civic engagement courses beyond the minimum requirement can vary greatly across schools depending on the school's funding and location.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And only schools that apply to the DOE can award the seal at all.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That means a student's chances of earning it can depend on which high school they attend, an issue I look forward to discussing today.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz recalls a 2023 joint hearing on the Seal of Biliteracy when CUNY said only Marist automatically awarded credit. He says today 10 CUNY colleges plus two schools award between three and eight credits for that seal, showing what collaboration can achieve.
chapters.title: Dinowitz compares Seal of Biliteracy credit success

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But three years ago this month, when I chaired the Higher Education Committee, we held a joint hearing like this with the Education Committee on the New York State Seal of Biliteracy, another seal awarded for

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: work including...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: testing, including service learning.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Students earn it by accumulating points through coursework, exams, and projects.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And at that hearing, CUNY told us that of the colleges it had researched across the state, Marist was the only one automatically awarding credit for that seal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But today, 10 CUNY colleges, along with the School of Labor and Urban Studies and the School of Professional Studies, award between three and eight credits for this seal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, that is what's possible when we work together, when we elevate these issues and elevate the really rigorous work that our students do in the classroom and incentivize our schools to do it through college credits from CUNY.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says the Seal of Civic Readiness has no downside for students. He calls it a win for students, families, DOE schools, CUNY campuses, and taxpayers.
chapters.title: Dinowitz calls Seal a five-way win

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I said at that hearing, it's not often in education that we find a program with no downside, no trade-off, no drawback.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'll say it again today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: For students, the seal of civic responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Readiness has no downside.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Recognizing and rewarding students'participation and success in civic projects and courses, both by DOE and CUNY, is a, I'm going to count them, win, win, win, win, win.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, you got all five, win, win, win, win, win.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's for students, families, DOE schools, CUNY campuses, and taxpayers of New York City.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says Res 418 calls on CUNY to ensure all campuses award appropriate college credits for the Seal. Proposed Res 620A calls on DOE to ensure the Seal is awarded in all NYC public high schools to eligible students.
chapters.title: Dinowitz presents Res 418 and Res 620A

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'm looking forward to hearing the details from our witnesses and, of course, everyone who's here today to testify.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Today, we'll also hear my two resolutions on the use and recognition of the seal of civic readiness.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Resolution 418 calls on CUNY to ensure that all campuses award an appropriate number of college credits to students who earn the seal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And proposed resolution...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: 620A calls in the DOE to ensure that the seal is awarded in all New York City public high schools to eligible students.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says the early work on the resolutions was done with students he mentored at Hunter College through the Grove Leadership Fellowship. He commends the CUNY students for drafting the resolutions as a civic project.
chapters.title: Dinowitz credits Hunter College Grove Leadership Fellowship students

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'm proud to say not only are these resolutions fantastic resolutions, but the early work on these resolutions was done with students I mentored at Hunter College, which is a CUNY school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They run a wonderful program, the Grove Leadership Fellowship, and civic leaders work with two to four undergraduate students on civic projects.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And our civic project was elevating civic education in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the path they took was drafting these resolutions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I want to commend those students and the work that was done by CUNY students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So now those

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: resolutions are being heard by these two committees today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I think that's a powerful civics lesson for all the students who are here today and are watching at home.

chapters.summary: Vine says CPL saves students time and money on the path to a degree and validates learning gained on the job, through training, or through lived experience. She says CPL sends a message to recipients that they are college material.
chapters.title: Vine defines CPL and its benefits

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: My name is Alyssa Vine, and I am the University Director of Credit for Prior Learning in CUNY's Office of Academic Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Credit for Prior Learning, or CPL, is an academic process by which CUNY's colleges can award academic credit for college-level learning acquired outside the traditional classroom.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: CPL is a nationally recognized strategy for recruitment and student success because it saves students time and money on their path to earning a degree.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: It also recognizes and validates their learning, whether it was gained on the job, through industry training, or through personal lived experience.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: CPL cultivates a sense of individual achievement and readiness for higher education, sending a message to its recipients that they are college material.

chapters.summary: Vine notes CUNY's CPL policy passed in 2020 and implementation work is ongoing. She says Res 418 asks CUNY to award credit for the Seal of Civic Readiness when there is alignment with college-level learning.
chapters.title: Vine describes CUNY CPL policy and Res 418 response

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Since CUNY's CPL policy was passed by the Board of Trustees in 2020,

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Implementation work has been ongoing, including and especially work to identify opportunities with system-wide potential to recruit and support populations of New Yorkers with high-demand skills and knowledge.

utterances.text: My testimony addresses how CUNY could respond to the call in proposed resolution 418

utterances.text: for college credit to be awarded to New York City public school students who earn the New York State Seal of Civic Readiness when there is alignment with college-level learning.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: CUNY sees potential in particular routes to the SEAL, especially the high school capstone project.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Determining whether the SEAL is eligible for college credit will require further faculty review and collaboration with New York City public schools.

chapters.summary: Vine says CUNY colleges award CPL for qualifying AP, IB, and Cambridge exams and are developing pathways for industry certifications. She also says 12 CUNY colleges have CPL pathways for Seal of Biliteracy recipients.
chapters.title: Vine lists existing CPL opportunities for high school students

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Before I expand on that, I will first provide context on existing CPL opportunities for students entering CUNY from the city's high schools.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: While CPL is often relevant for working adults who may be returning to college or enrolling for the first time, it is also a common and meaningful tool for students entering college from high school.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: There are numerous examples of CPL opportunities that are specifically targeted toward high school students, including several that are named in CUNY's CPL policy, such as

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: all CUNY colleges award CPL credit for qualifying scores on advanced placement exams, international baccalaureate exams, and Cambridge Advanced International.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: certificate of education exams.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Many CUNY colleges offer or are developing CPL pathways for key industry certifications, including credentials in IT, data analytics, and health and human services.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: High school students who earn these credentials through career and technical education programs in the city's high schools can receive the same CPL credit as working adults who earn these certifications for employment or career advancement.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Additionally, over the last several years, CUNY has been working to establish CPL opportunities for high school students who earn the New York State Seal of Biliteracy.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Currently, there are 12 colleges with CPL pathways in place for Seal of Biliteracy recipients, and work is ongoing to expand this to more colleges.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: These opportunities validate biliteracy with college credit and bolster pipelines for

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: related high need sectors, for example, teaching and nursing and healthcare shortages.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: This is the result of close partnership between CUNY's Office of Credit for Prior Learning and New York City Public Schools Office of Multilingual Learners.

chapters.summary: Vine says both seals recognize significant high school learning, but Biliteracy aligns with established language proficiency standards while Civic Readiness is broader. She says CUNY must examine evidence from particular pathways before awarding credit.
chapters.title: Vine compares Seal of Biliteracy and Civic Readiness for CPL

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: The seal of biliteracy offers a useful point of comparison because both seals recognize the significant learning completed in high school.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: For CPL purposes, however, the two seals present different assessment questions.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Biliteracy can be demonstrated against...

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Against established language proficiency standards, while civic readiness encompasses a broader

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: range of knowledge, skills, experiences, and forms of participation.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: From CUNY's perspective, the Seal of Biliteracy reflects a model of CPL assessment that is somewhat different from the topic of today's hearing, the New York State Seal of Civic Readiness.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: First, the Seal of Civic Readiness recognizes valuable learning and engagement across several pathways.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Because those pathways are intentionally varied, the learning demonstrated by SEAL recipients may not be uniform in content, depth, or alignment with a particular college course.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: The CPL question is therefore not whether civic readiness has value, but how CUNY can identify the routes and evidence that demonstrates college-level learning.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: The New York State Seal of Biliteracy provides a comparatively direct basis for CPL review because every recipient demonstrates language proficiency aligned with nationally recognized standards of the American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Language.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Civic readiness is broader by design and may be demonstrated through different combinations of coursework, projects, service, and other learning experiences.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: That breadth is a strength of the steel, but it also means that CUNY must examine the evidence associated with particular pathways before determining the appropriate award of college credit.

chapters.summary: Vine says the high school capstone project is a promising route for CPL because it may demonstrate advanced college-level learning. She suggests it may align with CUNY general education rather than a specific course or major.
chapters.title: Vine proposes capstone project review for college credit

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: One promising starting point is the rigorous high school capstone project with which New York City Public Schools has identified to us as an evidence of advanced and potentially college level learning.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: For CUNY CPL purposes, this route presents an opportunity with potential that's worth exploring.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Foundational knowledge of civics has broad value for college students.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: It connects multiple areas of the liberal arts and humanities while fostering social responsibility and civic engagement that are relevant across disciplines and career paths.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: For that reason, a CPL pathway tied to in-depth civic learning may align most appropriately with CUNY's general education curriculum rather than with a specific course or major.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: To determine whether the capstone project could support a CPL pathway, CUNY faculty would first need to review its requirements and implementation across participating high schools.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: They would need to confirm that the work is consistently demonstrating college-level learning, and if it does, they would need to identify appropriate CUNY courses or Pathways general education areas where that credit could be applicable.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Faculty could develop a rubric informed by the Seal of Civic Readiness model to assess students'capstone projects.

chapters.summary: Vine says CUNY faculty would need to review capstone requirements and implementation across high schools. She proposes a possible CUNY-specific civic readiness portfolio pathway and says CUNY wants to continue exploring with NYC Public Schools.
chapters.title: Vine outlines faculty review and CUNY-specific pathway

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Students meeting the established threshold would be eligible for CPL credit.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Another approach would be for CUNY faculty and New York City public schools to collaborate on a CUNY-specific seal of civic readiness pathway aligned with CUNY's pathway general education outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Students who complete a faculty-assessed civic readiness portfolio could be eligible for CPL credit.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: CUNY is interested in

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: continuing this exploration with New York City Public Schools, beginning with faculty review of the Capstone Project and other potential college-level routes to the SEAL.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: That process can advance the goal reflected in proposed Resolution 418 of recognizing civic readiness by cultivating a carefully designed pathway that could recognize meaningful student learning

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: while preserving the academic standards required for awarding college credit.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: For students arriving at CUNY, that recognition could do more than shorten the path to a degree.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: It can welcome them to the university by affirming that the knowledge, initiative, and civic commitments they developed in high school already have value in a college setting.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

chapters.summary: Cordelia Veve, DOE Chief of Curriculum and Instruction, introduces herself and colleagues Jenna Ryle, Chris Kermiet-Hall, and Superintendents Hoa Tu, Marcel Deans, and Anthony Inzerillo. She frames the hearing around implementing the NYS Seal of Civic Readiness.
chapters.title: Cordelia Veve introduces DOE team and context

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I'm going to take your lead and not lean over.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Denowitz, Chair Joseph, members of the Committees of Education and Higher Education, and distinguished members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: My name is Cordelia Vevey, and I am the Chief of Curriculum and Instruction for New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I'm joined by my colleagues, Jenna Ryle, Director of Civics, and Chris Kermie-Hall, Senior Curriculum Specialist, as well as Superintendents Hua Tu, Marcel Deans, and Anthony Anzarello.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to discuss the implementation of the New York State Education Department Seal of Civic Readiness, which is part of the NYSID Civic Readiness Initiatives and the proposed legislation.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: In New York City public schools, we believe that teaching the foundations of American government and the democratic process is vital to nurturing more engaged, active community members and informed potential voters.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Civics education should be an essential part of every student's core academic program.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: We are on our way to ensuring that every student in our schools has access to high-quality civics education, and the seal of civic readiness has been an important component of that growth.

chapters.summary: Veve says NYC Public Schools launched Civics for All in 2018 as part of Democracy NYC. She describes K-12 curriculum, school partnerships, participatory budgeting, student programming, teacher learning, and social studies comic books.
chapters.title: Veve recounts Civics for All history and resources

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: In order to place the seal in the appropriate context, it's helpful to know that New York City Public Schools first designed and implemented Civics for All, our civics learning initiative,

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: beginning in the spring of 2018, when it was announced as part of Mayor de Blasio's Democracy NYC plan.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: With the support of K-12 educators and New York City cultural institutions, the Department of Social Studies and Civics built a multifaceted initiative, including a K-12 curriculum,

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: school-based partnerships, a participatory budgeting program, student-facing programming, and teacher professional learning.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Beginning in 2020, an extensive collection of social studies and civic comic books supplemented these efforts.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Some people love them.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: These resources have been available to all schools in New York City public schools since their creation, with our team now supporting Civics for All implementation in 35 partner districts.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Our ultimate goal is to ensure that every single New York City public school student has access to high-quality civics education from kindergarten through 12th grade.

chapters.summary: Veve says the goal is high-quality civics education for every student K-12. She measures impact by access to curriculum, annual speeches on community issues, participatory budgeting, and civic action projects.
chapters.title: Veve describes goals and measures of civic learning

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: We measure our impact by accounting for students'access to opportunities to build civic knowledge through our Civics for All curriculum materials,

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: demonstrating civic skills by researching, writing, and delivering a speech each year on a community issue that matters most to them, practicing real-life democracy,

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: by engaging in participatory budgeting and engaging in civic action projects at least once per grade band.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: While the seal of civic readiness is an exciting and worthwhile way to honor our students'civic readiness upon their graduation, it is not the sole marker of civic learning.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Many more of our public school students are receiving comprehensive civics education across grades K through 12 than have already received the seal.

chapters.summary: Veve says NYC Public Schools joined the statewide Civic Readiness Initiative in 2018 and helped develop the definition and capstone. She lists the four domains: civic knowledge, civic skills in action, civic mindsets, and civic experiences.
chapters.title: Veve discusses statewide Civic Readiness Initiative and domains

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: The seal is a high priority, and we seek to offer all students the opportunity to earn it.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Our involvement with the statewide Civic Readiness Initiative began in the fall of 2018 when members of the New York City

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Public Schools Department of Social Studies and Civics were invited to join the task force that NYSID assembled to work on developing a statewide definition of civic readiness, the seal of civic readiness, and the capstone component of the seal.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: The finalized statewide definition of civic readiness includes four domains of civic readiness intended to be developed across grades K through 12.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Civic knowledge, civic skills in action, civic mindsets, and civic experiences.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: These domains undergird our K-12 continuum of civic learning and inform the elements of the seal of civic readiness as it was being designed.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Once established, the seal of civic readiness was approved by the Board of Regents in 2021 and piloted across the state, including in New York City Public.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: The launch of the NICID Seal of Civic Readiness complemented our citywide civics education initiative by offering a formal recognition that a student has demonstrated proficiency in the domains of civic readiness.

chapters.summary: Veve says students need six points, with two from civic knowledge and two from civic participation. She says schools can develop their own routes to the Seal using 11 criteria worth between 0.5 and 4 points.
chapters.title: Veve explains Seal point structure and school flexibility

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: In order to earn the Seal of Civic Readiness, a student must earn six points from a list of criteria that demonstrate a student's proficiency in civic knowledge and civic participation.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Two of a student's points must be from the civic knowledge criteria, two must be from the civic participation criteria, and the remaining two can be from either one.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: There are 11 possible criteria, each earning a student between 0.5 and 4 points.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: The intent behind this structure is to maximize the way a student's strengths and school experience can earn them points towards the SEAL.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: It allows schools to develop their own routes to the SEAL using those criteria, building on their school's distinctive context and existing programming, while also supporting students'needs aligned to their school's culture.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: For example, a school with a law program in which students take civics-related electives has the option to accredit these electives and ensure students can earn points by taking them.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: A school without walls, one of our New York City outward-bound schools that uses student-led individualized learning plans and integrates fieldwork and internships,

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: designed a multi-year civic readiness capstone project that incorporated portfolio-based assessments.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: used for exit requirements.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: The large number of participating high schools have developed a wide range of ways that students can earn the seal of civic readiness, each grounded in the domains

chapters.summary: Jenna Ryle, DOE Director of Civics, says schools must use pre-accredited projects or submit their own for accreditation. She says this process ensures Seal-related projects meet NYSED requirements and maintain rigor.
chapters.title: Jenna Ryle describes accreditation and rigor standards

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: of civic readiness and supported by the foundations of civic learning built through Civics for All programming, starting in the elementary grades.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: While this potential for customization is an asset, ensuring that as many students as possible have the opportunity to earn the seal, we also need to adhere to appropriate standards of rigor.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So we require schools offering the civics project, civic electives, or the capstone project to do so using a pre-accredited product or to submit a school-created version for accreditation prior to implementation.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: This process has ensured that our team can vet and accredit SEAL-related projects and programming that external organizations may have created to meet NISID SEAL requirements.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: From the initial rollout of the Seal of Civic Readiness, our Department of Social Studies and Civics created a system of support and guidance to successfully implement the seal, while allowing for the flexibility schools need to align their school's context.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: With the permission of NYSID, we created a local version of the Seal of Civic Readiness handbook, providing clear and detailed guidance for schools on each criterion of the seal.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Our goal is to ensure that every New York City public school receives the resources and support needed to implement the seal internally.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: While some schools do take advantage of external resources, including a subset of the resources that might cost something, all schools receive professional learning, curriculum resources, guidance documents, and support to implement.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: the seal.

chapters.summary: Ryle says DOE designed citywide professional learning and intensive school-based partnerships. She says the model shifted to district-based support as participation grew.
chapters.title: Ryle details two-tier professional learning and partner schools

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: The support that schools receive for the seal of civic readiness is incorporated into the overall Civics for All program.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Earlier, I mentioned the school-based partnerships that were part of the initial design of the Civics for All in 2018.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: While all civics curricular resources created at that time were sent to every New York City public school,

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: we knew that providing those resources without support for their implementation, particularly outside of a mandated content area, would not result in their widespread use.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So we designed a two-tier system of professional learning.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: One was available citywide for all schools to participate in, while the other was a more intensive school-based partnership model in which opting-in schools were provided with direct support from the members of the newly created Civics for All team.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: They did this to integrate into their teaching and learning they were already doing.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Once the seal became part of New York City Public Schools'civic education offerings, both tiers were updated to include support for its implementation.

chapters.summary: Ryle says partner schools grew from 103 in 2019-2020 to 196 in 2021-2022 before shifting to a district model. She says 35 of 45 districts now participate in the Civics for All Partner District Program.
chapters.title: Ryle reports growth in partner schools and districts

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: At its start, the long-term plan was to build those school-based partnerships until we had enough participation to shift to a district-based model.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: In our first full year, 2019-2020, we had 103 partner schools.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: That number saw a small dip to 96 in 2020-2021, while schools faced the uncertainty of the COVID-19 pandemic, before rebounding to 196 partner schools.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: That was also the year when the superintendents of District 25 and 26 decided that they wanted all of their schools to be partner schools after experiencing the positive impact of Civics for All during the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: From 2022 to 2023, we continued to support individual partner schools while bringing on additional districts before shifting to a full partner district model in 2024-2025.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Currently, 35 of New York City Public Schools'45 districts are part of the Civics for All Partner District Program, with many of the remaining 10 districts in an active building year preparing to join the program.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Each partner district identifies a point person in their district office who is paired with a Civics for All team member, and together they provide direct support toward implementing civics education to the schools in their district.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: While this model ensures the capacity needed to provide this direct support, the majority of the 10

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: non-partner districts have designated district points who work with the Department of Social Studies and Civics more broadly while helping to support social studies and civics work in their district.

chapters.summary: Ryle says Seal-offering schools grew from 31 in the pilot year to 271 in 2026-2027. She reports 12,019 students graduated with the Seal in 2025-2026, a 1,600% increase from 682 in the 2021-2022 pilot year.
chapters.title: Ryle reports Seal school and graduate growth

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We are very proud of how the number of schools offering the seal of civic readiness has grown.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: From 31 in our pilot year to 60 in 22-23, 118 in 23-24, 166 in 2020.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: 24-25, 230, and 25-26, and to our largest number yet, 271 and 26-27.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: At the end of the 25-26 school year, 12,019 students graduated with the Seal of Civic Readiness, a 1,600% increase in five years from this.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: 682 graduates who received the seal in 21-22 pilot year.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: This increase has been possible due to the New York City Public Schools'focus on a well-paced, strategic, and robustly supported effort to expand the number of students who have the opportunity to learn the Seal of Civic Readiness.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We fully expect to continue this deliberate rollout and expansion, seeking to significantly expand the number of schools offering the seal each school year.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We would like to thank the City Council for your continuous partnership in supporting civics education.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Whether you participated in school visits for Civics Week or joined our post-soapbox issue roundtables, we are grateful for your participation and advocacy in supporting students as they engage in civics and gain the skills needed

chapters.summary: Ryle says DOE supports collaboration with the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene on oral health education. She says DOE looks forward to working with the Council on distributing dental care and fluoride information to families.
chapters.title: Ryle addresses Int 259 dental care materials

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: to fully engage in a democratic society.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Finally, I will turn to the proposed legislation, Entry 259, which would require New York City public schools to collaborate with the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene to develop materials relating to the importance of dental care

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: and fluoride and distribute those materials.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We support the...

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: collaboration, allowing all students and families to receive oral health education, ensuring consistent and efficient use of the public health expertise.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the Council on how we identify the best methods for distributing important information to families to best support their health.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Thank you to the Council for the opportunity to speak today.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We look forward to your questions.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how many Seal recipients have come to CUNY and for demographic data, and whether CUNY admissions captures the state program service code. Alyssa Vine says CUNY does not currently consider the Seal in central admissions and will look further into it.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks CUNY about Seal data and admissions code

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'd like to recognize Councilmember Epstein, Ressler, and Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm going to head over to CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do you know how many students have come to CUNY with New York State Seal of Civic Readiness since the first seal was awarded in June of 2022?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do you have any data on students'demographic characteristics, including race, ethnicity, and income level?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Diploma and districts reported to the state under program service code 8313.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
