utterances.text: According to CUNY's Office of Enrollment Management, the Seal of Civic Readiness is not currently considered as part of central admissions, and they're not aware of it being used at college-level admissions.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: However, this is the purview of enrollment management, so I'm not aware of how or if it could be recognized, but we can look further into this and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So two assignments already, and we're just 10 minutes into this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Joseph notes CUNY's CPL policy is university-wide but faculty determine equivalencies. Vine says no CUNY colleges have evaluated the Seal of Civic Readiness yet, but CUNY looks forward to engaging faculty.
chapters.title: Joseph asks CUNY whether faculty evaluated Seal for credit

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In 2023, CUNY testified that credit for prior learning policy is university-wide, but that faculty at each CUNY college are responsible for determining CPL equivalencies and credit awards.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Has the faculty at any college CUNY evaluated the seal of civic readiness for credit?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Which college?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And what did they decide?

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: No CUNY colleges have evaluated the Seal of Civic Readiness at this time.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: However, we look forward to engaging faculty in the process of evaluating it and supporting their work to do so.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: In the near future.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks whether CUNY will create a working group or task force. Vine describes an existing model that brings faculty from about eight colleges together with materials and student work to make a system-wide recommendation.
chapters.title: Joseph asks CUNY about working group model for evaluation

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Does that mean putting a working group together to make it happen?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is that a task force within your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How does that, what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Yeah, so we have an existing model for coordinating collaborative evaluation of multiple CUNY colleges.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: We generally bring together faculty from around eight colleges to, and we support them by gathering all related materials, putting them in touch with experts on

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: the learning experience that they're evaluating, helping them in this case connect also with students who have earned the Seal of Civic Readiness, sample projects,

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: all the material to really help them understand the relevance of the Seal of Civic Readiness to college curriculum so that they can come up with a recommendation that then will be shared across all CUNY colleges for consideration and implementation.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks whether credit awards are publicized to prospective students. Vine says CUNY lists credit awards on a website and in the Transfer Explorer tool, and will do the same for Civic Readiness once colleges award credit.
chapters.title: Joseph asks CUNY how credit awards are publicized

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is that also publicized to prospective students coming into the CUNY system?

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Well, when we have coordinated system-wide evaluation of different learning experiences, once colleges have decided to award credit and those credit awards are in place,

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: For example, in the case of the seal of biliteracy, we have a website that lists all of the CUNY colleges that award credit and what those credit awards are.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Also, the information is entered into CUNY's student information system.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: So it is searchable in CUNY's public-facing searchable database, CUNY's Transfer Explorer tool.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: So that is available as well.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is that also for civic readiness or just for biliteracy?

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Well, at this time, since there aren't any colleges that are awarding credit for civic readiness, there aren't examples of that in place.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: But we definitely have a model for making sure that that information is publicized as soon as there are colleges that are awarding credit for it.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And how do you plan on, will that also be added to the website as you've done for the biliteracy?

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Yes, we would absolutely create a visible website where

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: students and high school counselors and teachers and families can find the information about where credit is available across the system.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks whether CUNY will publicize the benefits of earning the Seal once credit pathways are in motion. Vine says yes, CUNY is proud to help students save time and money toward degrees.
chapters.title: Joseph asks CUNY to publicize benefits of Seal

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The next question is going to be tricky.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we're going to work together to create this cohort and getting this out the door.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We're going to publicize it.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We're going to get the work done.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And when you do, do all of this.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You're going to publicize the benefits of earning a New York State Seal of Civic Readiness.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is that something CUNY plans to do once everything is in motion?

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: I would say that we are really proud of the opportunities that we create for New York City high school students and for New York City working adults to earn credit on their way into CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: It saves them time and money on their path to a degree.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: And we are always eager to make sure that people who are eligible are aware of that and able to take advantage of it and use it to benefit their education.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how many class of 2026 students earned the Seal and how many high schools offered it. Jenna Ryle says 12,019 students earned the Seal across 230 high schools.
chapters.title: Joseph asks DOE about 2026 Seal earners and school coverage

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: New York City Public Schools, how many students in the class of 2026 earned a New York State seal of civic readiness and how many high schools?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many students in total were in the class of 2026 and how many New York City Public Schools in total?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: In the 25-26 school year, we had 12,019 students earn the seal of civic readiness, and that was across 230 high schools.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is the plan to offer that in every high school?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What, is there a timeline?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We are actively pursuing 100% participation.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Right now we're in 56.2% of our diploma granting schools.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how many schools applied for 2026 and how many will offer the Seal. Ryle says DOE accepts all schools that apply and works with them to meet requirements.
chapters.title: Joseph asks DOE about Seal application process

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And the DOE application process for schools that want to offer the seal end in August, how many schools have applied in the 2026 school year and how many will offer the seal this year, do you know?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We accept all schools that apply.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So if a school applies and has not been able to answer the questions comprehensively, we work with them to do so so that they can offer the seal.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it over to Councilmember Dinowitz, and I will come back with other questions.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks how DOE tracks the number of students earning the Seal. Ryle says schools submit Seal earners as part of graduate data reporting, and numbers should match ATS discharge records.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks DOE how Seal earners are tracked

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I have like a, like it's a technical question.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So 12,019 students received the seal, 271 schools participated.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How are you tracking the number of students who earned the seal?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Feels like karaoke.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So as part...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We'll adjourn and then you can sing to your heart's content.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I mean, I take requests.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So as part of...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You can use your two minutes to make a request, Lincoln.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: It's going to be terrible and off-key.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: But so as part of graduate data reporting each year, all SEAL schools, and this is spelled out in the handbook,

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: submit to us any students who have earned the seal of civic readiness, and then that number is meant to match their sort of discharge record, so what's reflected in ATS.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says ATS only allows one seal and asks whether numbers are undercounted for students earning multiple seals. Ryle says there are no combination codes, but cumulative records should list all endorsements.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions ATS limitation on multiple seals

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I'm glad you said ATS because it was reported to us that ATS only allows you to list one seal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I guess biliteracy is worth more to a school score than civic readiness.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So if there is a student who earns two seals, they're only going to put biliteracy.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So two questions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: One is, are these numbers accurate or are they undercounted because there may be students who aren't able to be put into ATS?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And second, you're switching to...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: OASIS.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Once that transition is complete, will that allow for multiple seals to be included in the data that's reported out by the schools?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So to answer the first part of your question, we ask schools to report all students that earn the seal to us.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Currently, there are no combination codes for a student's transcript.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: However, schools are meant to produce a letter that goes in a student's cumulative record folder that includes all of the distinctions and endorsements that were placed on their diploma.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So, for example, if a student got the CDOS, the Seal of Biliteracy, and the Seal of Civic Readiness, even though the order of precedence, which is the document that tells the school how to discharge a student, might

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: tell them to give the student the CDOS in their transcript on that document in their cumulative record folder, it should include all three of those endorsements.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: But in terms of the coding, it's not there.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks whether the transition from ATS to OASIS will allow multiple seals in reported data. Ryle says DOE is building a civic readiness tracker in STARS Classroom and future coding depends on state guidance.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks about OASIS transition and combination codes

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So on the other part of your question, we are working with DIT to build a self-circumcision readiness tracker in Star's classroom, which will eventually evolve into OASIS.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I don't know what the plan is right now with combination codes, but I imagine with the portrait of a graduate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What's to imagine?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Or I imagine there will be updates to the way that things go because we'll get new guidance from the state.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Well, I hope so.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I wouldn't imagine.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You have the whole DOE here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I hope it's not imagining things.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, there's still a lot of unknowns in this portrait of a graduate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I just want to get, just stick with ATS for a second.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You are transitioning from ATS.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: TS to OASIS, you're not going to be using ATS anymore?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: That would be the Office of Policy and Evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I don't actually know the timeline for the transition.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I do know that they're developing OASIS.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But there is a transition.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: ATS, by the way, looks like it's MS-DAS.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And if you don't know what MS-DAS is, then that tells you everything you need to know about schools using ATS.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, so we'll follow up with that other department about switching to OASIS.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks whether DOE tracks which high schools offer civic participation opportunities and whether offerings differ by poverty level. Ryle says DOE does not have that data right now.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks DOE whether civic opportunities vary by poverty

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: To earn the seal, students need at least two points in civic participation, which come from civics projects, service learning, civic engagement, electives, extracurriculars, and work-based learning.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Does the DOE track which high school offers the individual opportunities?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And do those offerings differ by the school's poverty level?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I don't believe we have the data right now to know whether the offerings for the specific opportunities differ by the school makeup.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: But I think Chris can speak to the way that we are tracking what are the projects that each school is offering because either they are taking from

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: a vetted list of accredited projects or they are submitting a project for accreditation as part of their process for becoming a high school that offers the sealed civic readiness.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Yeah, so another part of our handbook for the seal for New York City public schools is our academic integrity procedure section.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And so that outlines the sort of accreditation policies that I'll be talking about, but to what Delia was just mentioning.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So we work with internal DOE offices and external organizations to accredit projects or electives for citywide use.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And those are available for any school to add to their school's programming.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: But schools also can develop 2A civics projects or 2C civics electives that they submit instructional materials to us for review for.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And we match those against the specifications in the handbook to accredit them or not, or the 2F capstone, which is more of a sort of planning document.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks about the content, depth, and rigor of Seal projects. Ryle says the handbook aligns every project to commencement-level standards and the accreditation rubric ensures consistent rigor.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks DOE about rigor of Seal projects

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to stay with that and talk about

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The projects, first of all, when we met with principals and teachers, they were very pleased with the way that the office runs and that you have these sample – it's not just you guys –

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: that you have these sample projects, things that are vetted and accredited.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I– Ms.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Fine, in your testimony, you had said–

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: that

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: These pathways are varied, and learning demonstrated by SEAL recipients may not be uniform in content, depth, or alignment with a particular college course.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And that touches on some of the concerns we have about the portrait.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Not its alignment to a specific course, but its content, depth, and alignment.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And alignment with a curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can you speak to the content and depth, and I'll use the word rigor as well, of these projects?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Are they all of the same rigor?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So the handbook lays out the commencement level standards that every project is supposed to align to.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And then the accreditation process and the rubric that goes for each project demonstrates how that project would align to those commencement level standards.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And so I think, you know, connecting it back to what you were talking about in terms of a portrait of a graduate, that maybe the pathway to the standpoint.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: can vary, but the actual demonstration and application of standards, knowledge, and attributes is going to be the same level based on that project.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: But those projects might look slightly different given the context of a school.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks whether DOE views the Seal as more rigorous than standard coursework. Ryle says she would not say more rigorous, but it offers multiple ways to demonstrate learning and can substitute for graduation requirements.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks if Seal is more rigorous than standard coursework

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We've been joined by Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So if it is adhering to a standard, does the DOE view the seal of civic readiness as more rigorous than the current standard coursework that a high school student takes?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I don't know that we would say more rigorous.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I think that we're saying, and the state would say, right, as well, because it can be a four plus one, that it can substitute for graduation requirements similarly to the regions exams.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: What it does offer is multiple ways to demonstrate that learning and show that application.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I think we could, you know, refer to one of our superintendents to talk about the ways that that looks different across different schools, but keeps the same level of rigor.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks whether the Seal is a multi-year project. Ryle says the Seal is a portfolio that can start with an eighth-grade capstone and continue through 12th grade experiences and projects.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks about multi-year portfolio nature of Seal

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it's a multi-year project, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: These are over the course of multiple years.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Students are engaging in this.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Yeah, so the SEAL is really a portfolio, right?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: It's like not one single thing.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: It's a combination of students'experiences starting even in eighth grade when they can have their middle school capstone and then going through ninth all the way through 12th grade where they may be earning.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: those points through different experiences, different coursework, and different projects that they're doing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, I want to come back to this, you know, the work, the rigor, and really getting it to a place where it'll get college credit that our students deserve.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: For now, I'm going to turn it back to the chair to call on council member for council member questions.

chapters.summary: Carl Wilson asks how civic knowledge can include harder parts of history like racism, homophobia, and sexism. Ryle says DOE curriculum uses multiple perspectives and a hard history series to support teachers.
chapters.title: Wilson asks DOE about teaching hard history in civic knowledge

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Councilmember Wilson?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you all for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So the seal of civic readiness requires two points in civic knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: What steps can we take to ensure that the civic knowledge includes an acknowledgement of the harder parts of our history,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: racism, homophobia, sexism, violence, and that students are not excluded from understanding the full scope of the nation's civic?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: history.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I'm just going to hold the whole thing here.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So for the students to demonstrate civic knowledge, some of the options are just social studies courses, the Regents exam, a civic knowledge project.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Through our office, which is the Department of Social Studies and Civics, we produce a social studies curriculum that the majority of the schools use.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: That curriculum is focused on multiple perspectives and ensuring that students are getting that 360-degree view of history.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I think our comic books that we share with you also support that effort.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We also provide professional learning to our teachers.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We have a hard history series, recognizing that for teachers, particularly social studies teachers, dealing with some of those harder aspects of history may feel easier to ignore than to address head on.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And so it's our effort to ensure that teachers feel supported in that work, that they have a framework and tools for doing so, and that the curriculum provides them the resources necessary to deal with all aspects of history.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks how DOE ensures civic engagement opportunities are equally accessible to all students. Ryle says DOE built in-house opportunities so the Seal does not depend on external resources that better-resourced students may access.
chapters.title: Wilson asks DOE about equitable access to civic engagement

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And some pathways to the seal of civic readiness will inherently be more accessible to students from certain backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So what can you do to ensure that the opportunity for civic engagement is equally accessible to everybody?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So one of the things that was a priority for us in building the seal of civic readiness and how that would be applied in New York City was recognizing that there are lots of opportunities external to New York City public schools that students could take advantage of to gain civic experience.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And that due to the civic empowerment gap, those are going to apply more to our students who are better resourced.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And so what we wanted to do was build a program that ensured that schools had everything they needed for the seal of civic readiness in-house through New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And then we also engage with external partners.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: But when we do that, we ensure that that is something that is available publicly to all schools citywide.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks how DOE engages immigrant students from different civic traditions. Ryle says the curriculum draws on students' lived experiences as assets, and Superintendent Deans will speak to family outreach.
chapters.title: Wilson asks DOE about engaging immigrant students

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And then my last question is many of our schools have large immigrant populations, immigrant student populations that are in many cases coming from countries with different civic traditions and forms of government.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So how do you work to engage them in the political process?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So I'll first say in terms of our civics curriculum, it really draws on students'lived experiences, and that's messaging that we provide to schools and professional learning as well,

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: that our students have diverse backgrounds, they have different lived experiences, and that those are assets, and they should be treated as such when we're talking about civics and civics education.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: In terms of how we're engaging families, I'd love to have one of our superintendents, superintendent deans, speak to what that looks like.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: While you exchange, I want to recognize Councilmember Farias.

chapters.summary: Marcel Deans, Bronx High School Superintendent for Districts 8, 10, and 11, describes parent outreach through a Bronx Museum Civics Fair. He says Seal earners in his district grew from 9 in 2022 to 780 in 2026, and notes over 78% of students are Title I.
chapters.title: Superintendent Marcel Deans describes Bronx parent outreach and Civics Fair

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: Got to turn the power on.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Dinowitz, for mentioning that to me.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: Marcel Deans, I'm the Bronx High School Superintendent for Districts 8, 10, and 11.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: I want to talk a little bit about parent outreach.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: At the school level, participating schools develop a SEAL program plan that includes how they will communicate with students and with families about eligible courses, projects, experiences, and the benefits of the SEAL.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: That's an important starting point.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: But in our district, we want to go beyond simply telling families the opportunity exists.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: We want them to see the learning and understand why it matters.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: One way we do that is through our annual Bronx Museum Civics Fair.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: Students bring their civic projects into a public space, present their thinking, and engage with families, community members, and cultural partners.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: Through relationships with institutions such as the Museum of the City of New York and the Intrepid, we are helping students see that learning extends beyond the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: And families get...

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: to see their children as researchers, as problem solvers, and young people with something meaningful to contribute.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: The growth has been encouraging over the years.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: We went from nine students earning the seal in 2022 to 780 young people in June of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: And getting back to Chair Dinowitz's question earlier, we're a district with over 78% Title I.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: And so our economically challenged families and young people are benefiting.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: Greatly and deeply from this work.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: But I do want to use, I do not want us to confuse growth in numbers with full measures of success.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: The real question is whether more students, including multilingual learners and students with disabilities, are consistently experiencing this level of rigor, rigorous and relevant learning.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: For us, outreach is also about making those opportunities visible, making those opportunities valued, and increasing accessibility for the families that we serve in Bronx North.

utterances.speaker: Marcel Deans
utterances.text: Well, I won't call it Bronx North because it's Northeast, but Bronx High School Districts 8, 10, and 11.

chapters.summary: Phil Wong asks what the Seal translates to in college credits and how students are informed. Alyssa Vine says no CUNY colleges award credit yet, and Cordelia Veve describes future CPL credit setup. Wong also asks how DOE will reach schools not offering the Seal; Veve says DOE will keep engaging superintendents and principals.
chapters.title: Wong asks CUNY and DOE about Seal credit and school outreach

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Council Member Wong.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'm reading this right now, and it says, in order to earn the seal of civic readiness, a student must earn six points from a list of criteria that demonstrates the student's proficiency in civic knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So what does that translate to in terms of college credits, and how do you inform that to the student?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because not all schools offer these.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Civic, CEO of Civic Readiness.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please answer that.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: So at this time, there aren't any CUNY colleges that are awarding credit for the seal of civic readiness.

utterances.speaker: Alyssa Vine
utterances.text: However, once we have faculty evaluate the seal and determine its alignment with curriculum or general education and implement a specific

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: the CIFIC CPL Credit Award.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: That CPL Credit Award will be established in the student information system so that any student who presents appropriate documentation or once we have data sharing in place, students will be able to receive those credits.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My second question is not every school is offering this state seal of civic readiness.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So how are you going to, how does DOE plan to do outreach and let other schools know or let the students know here are the schools that have it and then, you know, work on the other schools that don't have it?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I think you just told us our strategy.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: So we have grown year over year with schools that are offering the Seal of Civic Readiness.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Superintendent Deans just spoke to the great growth that he saw in his district.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: And that is our intention to keep engaging superintendents and principals to see where they see the value and work with them in order to design the learning for students in their schools.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Joe.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Council Member Brewer?

chapters.summary: Gale Brewer praises Civics for All programs and asks how the Youth Civic Hub and about 100 youth groups fit into civics education. She complains that the public often believes schools do not teach civics and asks what publicity DOE is doing.
chapters.title: Brewer praises Civics for All and asks about Youth Civic Hub and publicity

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have been to, I think, all of the civics for all programs in my district, and phenomenal.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, memorizing Abraham Lincoln's inauguration speech.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So it's phenomenal.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I can't say how great it is.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My question is, having done Teens Take the City for 100 years and been

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: working with Generation Citizen and done voter registration and PB and every other thing I can think of in the schools and put young people on community boards, put young people on the CECs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Right now I'm...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Put max on all of them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My question is, when I look at the youth civic hub, which has, I don't know, it looks like about 100 different groups on it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how do they play a role in all of this?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's number one.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then the second thing is, if I have one more freaking person come up to me at Fairway and say, the schools don't do civics.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question to you, no, really, I'm serious.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm so sick of it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then I have to spend 20 minutes at the coffee place right there while I'm trying to get my damn coffee explaining to them what you do.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So you really, really, really, because don't forget, not everybody's a public school parent.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Not everybody knows the schools like we do.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And the private schools do civics.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have Spence kids.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have Dalton kids.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have every intern known to humankind.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so my question is, you have.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Got to tell people what you're doing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Really, it's to the point that nobody knows.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They literally believe that not one minute of civics is taught in the public schools.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I would like to see what publicity you're doing on this topic.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Kamara needs to talk about it more, fine.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But you need to do more.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: He set it up in our area.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What are we going to do?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There's 100 groups.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you get them?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just looked at the list.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Not all of them do civics.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So you have to, I would like some kind of metrics, how they can help.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because they all think they're helping.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't know if they really are.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So they do the best.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: With all due respect to everybody else, they do the best.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But you can work with others.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I want to know how you're working with all those 100 groups and how can they help?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because they're out there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're doing the same thing or they're trying.

chapters.summary: Jenna Ryle says DOE met with Youth Civic Hub organizers and shares the hub with schools. She describes internal awareness-building and external panels, but Brewer pushes for more public outreach.
chapters.title: Ryle responds on Youth Civic Hub and public messaging

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I think you and I both are at the same level of exhaustion of regularly telling people we do, in fact, teach civics in New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And so I think, well, first off, you mentioned the Youth Civics Hub.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So I do want to address that.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: If I'm correct, that is the website that was done in collaboration across a few youth civics ed organizations.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And so that's something we've met with those organizations to support them in that work.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We share it out to our schools so that the students know and have access to that youth civics hub when it was first being built.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I'm trying to.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: To recall, it was quite some time ago.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I had met with the students who were building it to talk through what we thought would be most accessible to students in schools.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So we're grateful to them for kind of taking that extracurricular piece so that students are aware of opportunities that they have available to them in their communities.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: In terms of messaging, I think, number one, our superintendents and their awareness.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: For us, too, when we first started implementing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I love the superintendents, but they don't go outside public schools.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They stay right in them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm just saying.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I love you guys, but don't do the outreach.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I think there was first some misunderstandings at the school level, at the superintendency, as to how civics would fit into the teaching and learning that was already happening.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And so we engaged in an internal New York City Public Schools-focused awareness-building campaign in those early years.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: As far as externally, I am often on panels that I am invited to.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: The Bar Association is one that I am on every year.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: New York Law School had a Constitution Day, just trying to get the word out.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Anytime someone says to me, we do not teach civics in New York City public schools, I give them my email address and tell them, invite me.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I'm happy to share that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yeah, but you can't do it with 8.4 million people.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I do my best.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I know, but we have to do more.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I'm just saying.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't know if the mayor wants to do his thing, but everybody, you know, Kamala could do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Somebody has to really tell people on a constant basis because it would help schools, our administration, our caring about the issue, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I would suggest if you can do something in the next few weeks.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Just so people know that it's, you know, it's a current topic, needless to say, in the United States right now.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I appreciate your passion for it.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And also thank you to both chairs for having this hearing in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I think this is doing a lot to build awareness.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how groups like Teens Take the City and Generation Citizen fit into Civics for All and whether they duplicate efforts. She requests metrics on how those groups help.
chapters.title: Brewer asks how external civics groups fit into Civics for All

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But how do groups like Teens Take the City, Generations, how do they fit into Civics for All?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How does it?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Work in terms of more cohesive so people aren't off doing the same thing and duplicating.

chapters.summary: Ryle says DOE encourages schools to collaborate with local civics organizations and sends a newsletter with opportunities. She says external organizations can accredit projects, citing YVote as an example.
chapters.title: Ryle explains external partner accreditation and newsletter

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Yeah, so external partners have a number of opportunities and ways that they can engage with schools.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: First off, while we provide everything that a school could need to build the seal of civic readiness through New York City public schools, we do encourage them to collaborate with civics education organizations that may be local to them.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: In terms of citywide, we have a newsletter that we send out to all of our schools with those opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And then also external organizations can accredit projects that they do with students for the seal of civic readiness.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So an example would be YVote right now.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I just had a conversation with their executive director a few weeks ago, and they are planning to submit the project that they do with students in their extracurricular program for accreditation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't want to keep more time, but could you send us a newsletter to see if I like it?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Happy to do that.

chapters.summary: Joseph thanks Brewer and says they often discuss how to get the message to families. She notes NYC Public Schools prints many comic books but families, students, and colleagues often do not know, and urges highlighting the best of public schools.
chapters.title: Joseph and Brewer discuss public messaging and comics

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And Councilmember Brewer and I, as she mentioned, that's something we talk about all the time.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do you get the messaging out to families that this is happening?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We don't know what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I know what's happening.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I also know that New York City Public Schools is one of the agencies that print the most comic books in the country.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But guess what?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The families don't know that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The students don't know that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: My colleagues don't know that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I do because I make it my business to know.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But we need to do a better job in promoting what New York City Public School is doing best.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We always see the worst of New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How about we start highlighting the best of New York City Public Schools?

chapters.summary: Amanda Farías asks how DOE teaches electoral and governmental civics, including voter pre-registration and understanding the two-party system. She says community members often think young people are not engaged in voting.
chapters.title: Farías asks about electoral and governmental civics instruction

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Councilmember Farias.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And apologies if this was discussed earlier in this way.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We've had several hearings today that I've had to pop in and out of.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I just want to get a better idea of how, even if adjacently, we're teaching electoral and governmental civics to students through this programming.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I hear, and I want to reiterate what all of my colleagues are saying, when we go in community, people are coming to us, and their initial thought of hearing civic engagement always directly aligns to voting power and electoral power

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: and how they don't think young people are engaged in that way or being auto-enrolled or understanding our two-party system in New York State and how there's influxes across the tri-state and the nation.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So can you help me?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: better understand how we're encouraging that since this is K through 12 and we are, we know folks can, young people can enroll early into their voter registration status and then, you know, be ready to vote when they're 18.

chapters.summary: Ryle says elections instruction starts in second grade and the high school civics curriculum includes a section called Vote with 18 activities. She says Civics Week in March includes a citywide student voter registration drive.
chapters.title: Ryle details elections curriculum and Civics Week registration

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: First, our education effort.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So there's both the social studies curriculum and the civics curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: I think recognizing that the social studies curriculum really covers, due to state standards, a lot of the foundational understanding of American government.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And then civics is supporting students in understanding how does that system impact them and how do they impact it.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So we start second grade is the first time that students are given explicit instruction on elections.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So second grade is the first time that they're given explicit instruction on elections and how those work.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And then as we move through the grades, there is very specific instruction on the levels of government, the branches of government.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: When we're talking about electoral power, our ninth through 12th grade civics for all curriculum has five sections.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: The fifth section is called Vote, an Instructional Guide to Elections.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And it has 18, I believe, suggested activities and lessons for teachers to engage students in that speak not only to the power of being a voter, but the ways you can have an impact on elections without being a voter as well, since that's what's relevant to the majority of our students.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And then we have Civics Week every year.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: It's the second week of March.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And that's when we register our students.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We have a citywide student voter registration drive.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: There are lots of schools that register students at different times of the year.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: That's our citywide push.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So when the age to pre-register was lowered to 16, we really pushed that citywide effort.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And we ensure that that is getting to all of our schools by paying teachers to coordinate that at the school level so that they are spending some additional time on that to make sure that all of the eligible students are registered, but also more importantly, that all of our students are being informed.

chapters.summary: Farías says she has participated in Civics Week but wants more comprehensive understanding of city efforts. She asks to receive electoral comics and participate more broadly in March; Ryle agrees to share materials.
chapters.title: Farías follows up on community engagement and Civics Week

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: That's really great to hear.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I've participated with schools in my district for Civics Week, but I don't think I've comprehensively received an understanding on what the city is doing.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And I think that goes to this beat that we keep drumming of it's not getting into community, how active or proactive we're being on civic education in our school system particularly.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: But, I mean, this is also more comprehensive involving community members, like our teachers, our community members that are staying after school.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: They're heading our music program and after school program and dance club and all of those sorts of things that they're touching

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: based with students in different capacities during this time frame as well so I'd love to stay engaged on that I'd love to get whatever comic book is for specifically for the electoral yeah there's quite a few on voting side

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: this feels there's education pieces here too but I'd love to see some of the electoral stuff and be able to participate in March with you folks more broadly in my district if we can.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We'll definitely get you our registered comics and thank you for joining our schools during Civics Week.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how many parents know their 16-year-olds can pre-register to vote. She says DOE must engage families where they are, including hair salons and churches.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about parent awareness of 16-year-old pre-registration

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Quick follow-up on that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many parents know that their 16-year-olds can pre-register?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That's also something I've talked about.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do we make partners with families?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: They are also part of this educational journey, and I think we don't engage families enough.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I think that should be something.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And you know where folks are also?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In hair salons, in churches.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I think we have to meet communities where they are.

chapters.summary: Mercedes Narcisse asks who decides what counts as civic action. Ryle says civic action projects are process-based and the topic comes from students themselves.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks who decides what counts as civic action

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Councilmember Narcisse?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I apologize that I have to move back and forth.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I don't know if that was asked before.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Who decides what counts as civic action?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So we have in our curriculum guides when we are encouraging schools to engage in civic action, it is process-based.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And so supporting teachers and understanding what are the steps they need to take to engage students in civic action projects, but what the students want to take civic action on comes from the students themselves.

utterances.text: Can working as a poll worker or running a voter pre-registration drive at a school count towards you?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Students who engage in extracurricular activities for a total of 40 hours and then write an application of knowledge product can count that extracurricular work towards the seal of civic readiness.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Does a summer youth employment program placement

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Oh, I already see.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because I mean, I love young people.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So they're giving their time.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I want to make sure that we can make sure that they know.

chapters.title: Narcisse comments on incentives and acknowledgement for youth

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The educational part within our school structure.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: When the parents, like when they're doing parents engagement in the school, I think it will be a good way to give it to the parents.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Sometimes, you know, our kids can be a little, I don't want to call them lazy, but they can be like a less fair attitude.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I think it would be a good idea to make sure that parents'night and whatever, where the parents are, to be engaged and knows what the extra things the kids can do.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Since I don't want my time to be like bing, bing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Just like for the credit.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I still have time?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Oh, that's good.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: High five.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: First, I want to say thank you for this young lady over here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how Civics for All will play a role with Portrait of a Graduate and how the Black Studies curriculum ties in. She notes the committees want cultural competence and students seeing themselves in curricula.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us.

chapters.summary: Ryle says the Seal allows students to demonstrate Portrait competencies like global citizen and critical thinker. She says DOE created a crosswalk linking social studies units, Civics for All lessons, and Black Studies curriculum.
chapters.title: Ryle explains Portrait connections and Black Studies crosswalk

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So for that first question, with Portrait of a Graduate, Portrait of a Graduate is the holistic explanation of what a graduate should have experienced by the time they graduate high school.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: What both Civic Readiness and specifically the SEAL of Civic Readiness does is allow for the vehicle for the student to demonstrate those things.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So we see the closest connection to global citizen, critical thinker, and effective communicator.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Obviously, there's connections to the others as well.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: But this is really an opportunity that our students are already engaged in to demonstrate that commencement level competency through project-based assessments.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: That was your first question.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Your second question.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So the Black Studies is a study of the world curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We have a crosswalk.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So we have designed our Passport to Social Studies curriculum and the Civics for All curriculum in-house.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: What we've created for schools to be able to implement all of those things, because we recognize that's a lot of material to be giving to a teacher.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So first we have a crosswalk that details the social studies units that schools are beholden to.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: under the state social studies framework.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And then for each of those units, it includes the lessons from Civics for All that are most relevant there, and then where the lessons from the Black Studies as a study of the world curriculum make sense in terms of the units of study.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We also, through our work with our district points, have been supporting them in thinking about that work as well.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph

utterances.text: We want to make sure that you're incorporating those.

utterances.text: When we talk about curriculums and students seeing themselves in those curriculums that we teach across the city.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Students are seeing exactly what's happening in our country and how can they have a voice in that process so they should be engaged in that process.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And our children need to feel, and especially for us, like we old people, we all right.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks about the DOE bank of vetted projects and auditing process. Cordelia Veve says the next step is for CUNY faculty to review actual student work products to establish credit pathways.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks about CUNY-DOE collaboration on project rigor

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to ask more about the CUNY-DOE relationship.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Because what I've heard, again, from principals and teachers, and that you've testified to, is you have sort of a bank of projects that students can work, or schools can engage with and students can work on.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And you've started auditing some of those projects.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like looking at some of the graded material?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So there's the two different processes.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: There's the accreditation process to ensure that the project that the school is using is approved by us and meets the standard of rigor.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And then there is an auditing process.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: To ensure that the output is of quality.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What precludes CUNY from looking at those projects and working more closely to say, yeah, these are actually very rigorous projects and conducting audits with them to say, you know what, this is college level work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so we should be accrediting our CUNY students with appropriate amount of college credits.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I think that is exactly what we need to do next is we need to see those products, the projects from the students.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: We need to have our faculty really closely.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's for someone else.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: You still have time.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I think that seeing the actual work products.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Now someone's just trolling you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Someone's having fun.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I think that seeing the actual work products of students and seeing how they reflect the components of the seal of civic readiness and having CUNY faculty.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Take a close look at that and understand the learning that it represents is the work.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: That is what we need to do in order to establish credit pathways for students who earn the seal of civic readiness.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz describes a symbiotic relationship where DOE shows what it is doing and CUNY says what it needs. He asks for a meeting on the calendar, and Veve agrees.
chapters.title: Dinowitz calls for CUNY-DOE meeting on credit pathways

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, it is a real symbiotic relationship.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The DOE is saying, here's what we're doing, and CUNY should be saying, hey, here's additionally what we need, not just for college credit, by the way, but what we need our high school students to be, the skills we need them to graduate with.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And those are conversations I think you have.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the seal of civic readiness should absolutely be part of it because the ultimate goal is to make sure students who are doing this rigorous work with vetted projects.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: With audited outputs from the DOE, the ultimate goal is for them to get the credit for the work that they're already doing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can we, can we,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Get a meeting on the calendar.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can we do, you have your peoples here.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Yes, we can absolutely have a meeting.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, because that was one of the hurdles that you mentioned in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so obviously, to me, it seems that meeting about the projects and the work the students are doing is, to me, the obvious next step.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Happy to participate in that meeting, but we do have a lot of CUNY and DOE people here as well.

utterances.text: You mentioned training a lot.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can you please share how much DUE spends annually to support implementation of the CO,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: the cost for participating school and per CO recipient, and the breakdown of the budget for the CO, including professional development?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: So we don't break down our budget by the seal as it's part of our larger effort around civics for all.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: So we can tell you that the overall civics budget is $3,001,659.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Of that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, I'm laughing because that's very specific.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: It's very specific.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Of that, and I think this might give you a more clearer sense of how that goes directly towards the seal,

utterances.text: is that 1.6 million of that is sammed out to schools for participatory budgeting.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: And that is one of the projects that can be used, one, for civics for all experiences for students, but also to be counted towards SEAL.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How much of– I didn't mean to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: And then professional learning.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That was, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.text: So the professional learning isn't necessarily, we don't break it out specifically to like these are SEAL

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: professional learning versus our overall professional learning for civics, which is inclusive of professional learning for districts and schools that are implementing the SEAL.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: And for that, we spend $861,770.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Specific again.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I like it.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: A nice round number.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How many cents?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: No cents.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks how much professional learning funding goes to private for-profit contractors. Ryle says Mikva Challenge is paid for Project Soapbox, while the rest of professional learning is provided by DOE's nine-person civics team.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks how much professional learning goes to contractors

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How much of that, let's say just the professional learning, for example, how much of that goes to private for-profit contractors or contracts versus in-house?

utterances.text: So that professional learning budget is for professional learning and curriculum and resource development.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So the majority of it would go to partners like Mikva Challenge, who supports our project Soapbox Work.

utterances.text: And then also our professional learning sessions we often do in collaboration with cultural institutions around the city.

utterances.text: And then for curriculum and resource development.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So I can't break down for you right now, like how much is spent on each of those things, but all of that funding is for the professional learning.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: There's separate funding for the creation of like our materials that get used in professional learning, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So to ask in a different way, how much money goes to...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Are you spending money on private companies to come into schools and train teachers?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Zero dollars and zero cents.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Mikva Challenge is the, to the best of my knowledge, and I will double check this in my budget, the organization that we pay to provide professional learning because Project Soapbox is their product.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: The rest of our professional learning is provided by our nine-person civics for all team.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'll share, speaking with some of the teachers, they were very grateful that their work, they would get per session for their work, whether it was like the working on the weekends or

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: turnkeying the learning that they did.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And, you know, it's less expensive to hire our very own teachers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But when they get that money, that's really recognizing their work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They feel seen and recognized for the work that they do.

utterances.text: I worry that as we seek to expand the seal of civic readiness, and as we seek to incorporate civics into the portrait of a graduate, it will be very tempting for the DOE to do what they often do is to hire outside contractors

utterances.text: to do the work that our teachers are going to do a better job at.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And you're going to keep the money in-house and keep the money for our teachers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I would urge you to ensure that as you grow and expand, keeping all of that professional learning, all of that curriculum development as in-house as possible

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
