chapters.title: Dinowitz asks DOE about longitudinal tracking of Seal earners

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I know CUNY does not track this, but does the DOE track students who've earned the New York State Seal of Civic Readiness and track longitudinally how they're doing in college or in career post-graduation?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Currently, we do not formally track that, but we are looking forward to doing more of that work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, is that on your agenda to do?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Which is part of the reason why we want to have the data tracking in STARS, which will enable us to better be able to see who are those students, what schools are they coming from.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks how journalism can become part of the approved civics project list. Chris Kermiet-Hall says there is a public accreditation portal where organizations can submit instructional materials for review.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks how journalism can count as civics project

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How can journalism become a part of the standard list of civics project approved by the DOE?

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: We have an accreditation portal, a forum where anyone can submit instructional materials for review, including external or internal organizations, and then we'll connect those

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: folks to get whatever the materials are accredited.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's a public website?

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: Yeah, I can.

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: Forward you the link.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we have, you know, Councilmember Joseph and I, for the first time, we got significant funding for youth journalism this year.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I know Councilmember Joseph was working on that for years.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We finally got funding this year, $285,000.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Sounds right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Maybe also $744 additional dollars.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But, you know, this is the type, especially as we move into the portrait, that we want to be encouraging.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And journalism is so deeply tied to civics that we want to make sure that that work is recognized for the seal of civic readiness.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz notes new youth journalism funding and says journalism is tied to civics, then turns the floor back to Chair Joseph.
chapters.title: Dinowitz turns back to Chair Joseph

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm going to turn it back to Chair Joseph now.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how DOE reaches parents and students whose first language is not English. Ryle says schools must create universal accessibility plans and Seal projects can be completed in home languages.
chapters.title: Joseph asks DOE about language access for Seal

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Denowitz.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Just want to do a couple of follow-ups from Chair Denowitz.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In terms of language access, how are we accessing parents who or students that English is not their first language?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So when schools are offering the seal of civic readiness, they have to create a program plan.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And one of the steps of that program plan is a universal accessibility plan.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: So how are they going to ensure that the seal of civic readiness is available to all students?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Secondary to that, and we don't have many schools yet taking advantage of this, but it is something that we regularly meet with the team who runs the seal of biliteracy.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Students who do their seal of biliteracy project.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: On a civics topic, that can be applied, we don't, you know, in any language, to the SEAL of civic readiness.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: Also students'soapbox speeches, which is another project that they can do for the SEAL, those can also be done in home language as well.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many people know that?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: That's what we're working with the team with the seal of biliteracy to match up the schools that are doing both programs.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That's where we, Councilmember Brewer and I, we're talking, always people walking up to us and asking us these questions.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: New York City public schools feel like this big black hole.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: No one knows what's happening, but amazing things are happening, but no one never knows about it unless you come to a hearing or someone else talks about it.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Chair Dinowitz will talk about it.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we got to do better.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And that's something I've been asking for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I think we got to do better.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how DOE supports schools that want to offer the Seal. Chris Kermiet-Hall describes cross-school sharing, and Superintendent Hoa Tu says Queens North doubled Seal schools year over year to 96%.
chapters.title: Joseph asks how schools support each other in offering Seal

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do schools support?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do schools support each other?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Let's say my school wants to open.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do we support that school that want to have a SEAL, civic readiness SEAL?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I think Chris wants to take this one.

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: It's actually one of the most awesome parts about supporting districts and schools with SEAL work is that

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: Oftentimes, so we'll assemble whole districts for the start of the year orientation.

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: And so there's a lot of really wonderful cross-pollination and cross-school support happening.

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: So if my colleague at another school has a project that they've accredited that I'm really interested in using, I'll carry that over and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: And I actually think Superintendent, too, could comment more on this.

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: If you'd like to, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: So what I would share is in Queens North, we have 25 high schools.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: And I'll answer it in two ways.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: One is setting up the expectation that the Civic Seal is an obligation of all of our schools to provide students with the opportunity to engage, to learn, not the knowledge, and then also to do the actual civic engagement work.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: The second to that is once we set that expectation, now school's on the hook to develop their programs and their service learning opportunities beyond the school walls.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: I know Jenna talked about we want to bring it into the schools so that all students have access.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: We actually in Queens North encourage our principal to reach across their school walls into their colleagues and beyond the borough for opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: So to date, I would say we have doubled the number of schools offering Civic Seal year over year to now 96% of our schools.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: And not because they didn't want to, that they said this is important for us to do and we are committed to learning from each other.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: And every month when we have our principal meeting, that is the forum and the venue where our principal openly share.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: Because the answer is always in the room.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: We don't need to go look for other people.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: I think, Chair, then it was to your point, we don't have to pay.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: other people for information when we have it.

utterances.speaker: Hoa Tu
utterances.text: But what we need to do as a system is to create the space or the stage, if you will, for us to ask the question and get the answer.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how DOE measures success and whether students give feedback on projects. Veve says success is measured by access and schools refine projects based on student and district learning.
chapters.title: Joseph asks how DOE measures success and uses student feedback

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I'm hearing a lot of turnkey.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We learn from each other to make sure that we're keeping the financial.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do you measure the success?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do you do?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there surveys at the end of the projects?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do students give feedback if, let's say, the project is not working or they don't like what you're offering?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How is their voice used in shaping this project?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: So I think first is we're measuring our success through access, right?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: We talked about expansion.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Are we including all students in this?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: We're working towards that.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: And then I think at each school, that is their work to refine the project.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Because I think, again, just remembering that the seal is flexible in design and in purpose, right?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: And that just because you did the seal exactly one way last year, the idea is that you could refine that, right, based on whether you hear that from students in your school

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: or like Superintendent, too, is talking about you've learned something from your colleagues in your district or even you've learned outside of your district.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I think that is one of the other benefits of the seal is.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: While it is flexible in design by individual school and district, the construct of it is the same, and so that I can adapt what's going on in one school to the next, to the next, and then

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: make it better each year and learn from it.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And any of those datas are used to drive?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Perfecting the program.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I hear expansion, but I also want to hear outreach.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I want to hear partnership.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I want to hear agencies are talking to each other.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Folks don't like to talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I find that very weird.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm an educator.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Teachers talk all day long to each other.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But I'm finding that institutions and agencies in the city are horrible at doing that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I'm hoping that CUNY and New York City public schools reach out and have that conversation around how can we perfect it.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And New York City public school is handing over their students and they're coming prepared to you.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks whether the Seal can substitute for a Regents exam. Chris Kermiet-Hall says it can substitute for the fifth Regents exam as a graduation pathway if students have ELA, math, social studies, and science.
chapters.title: Joseph asks whether Seal can substitute for Regents exam

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I had another question around, can the civic be substituted for a regent?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In lieu of a regent, you can do the civic readiness seal instead.

utterances.speaker: Chris Kermiet-Hall
utterances.text: Yeah, so it's a graduation pathway, so it can substitute for the fifth regent's exam, assuming you have one ELA, one math, one social studies, and one science.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You hear that?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But the regents are going away soon.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Bye-bye, regents.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Good riddance.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The parents are going to come for you.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how DOE informs middle school students about the Seal and how many seventh and eighth graders completed a capstone. Ryle says she will get the number.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about middle school capstone and Seal awareness

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I had, we wanted to talk quickly around middle school.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: There was something I saw around middle school that I wanted to talk about real quick.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You have that question?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yeah, 15.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Students in seventh and eighth grade earn one point toward the seal through middle school capstone project.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How does DOE inform middle school students about the seal?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many seventh and eighth graders completed a middle school capstone project last year?

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: We can get that number for you.

utterances.speaker: Jenna Ryle
utterances.text: And I think Superintendent Inzerillo can speak to how students are made aware about that middle school capstone.

chapters.summary: Anthony Inzerillo, Superintendent for District 26 elementary and middle schools, describes soapbox speeches and civic action projects for all middle schoolers. He says DOE shares opportunities through parent workshops, newsletters, CEC meetings, and district leadership teams.
chapters.title: Superintendent Inzerillo describes middle school capstone and outreach

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairs Joseph Dinowitz and committee members.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: Great to be here.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: In sixth, seventh, and actually eighth grade, and by the way, my name is Anthony Inzerello.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: I'm the superintendent for elementary and middle schools across District 26.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: I have to tell you, I'm so proud of the work that takes place across all of our middle schools.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: Across District 26, we give every single 6th, 7th, and 8th grader an opportunity to be able to research and develop

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: a soapbox speech where they can research a concern, a passion, something that they see an inequity about.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: They will then research it.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: They will develop a soapbox speech and not just share it with their class, but share it with the community.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: We have across our middle schools and also elementary schools where we have kindergarten students, middle school students sharing those soapbox speeches, which then leads into some of the other civics work like participatory budgeting and then some of the take action projects as well.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: So for middle school, part of them receiving the one point toward that credit

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: is we provide the opportunities for all middle school students to be able to have that opportunity and do that.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: So whether that's sharing those opportunities through parent workshops.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: principal newsletters, community educational council meetings.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: We have president's council meetings where we share that, district leadership team meetings.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: I send out newsletters to families as well.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: So we try to publicize it and make everyone aware of that as well.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: So even when our middle school students go home,

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: We want parents to ask their children, so what are you studying?

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: What are you passionate about?

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: What are you concerned about?

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: We want those conversations to be taking place at the dinner table.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: And then it's a great opportunity then for parents to be able to talk about their culture, their history, what they're passionate about, and then extend those conversations at home as well.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks whether schools talk about the Seal at open houses and whether the old big book of schools still exists. Veve says the big book is gone and information is now on MySchools.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about Seal promotion at high school open houses

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And the schools that, for example, I know it's high school season now at the open house.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do schools talk about that civic seal, the seal at the open house?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I know they used to give out a big book.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do you guys still give out that big book for kids to look through to pick out of school?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I don't think that big book exists anymore.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I think it's all transferred over to my schools, which I think brings up the point of why that information needs to be available through that digital portal.

chapters.summary: Inzerillo says District 26 has a high school fair on November 9 and he will add a marker or asterisk for schools with strong civics programs. He says families should see civics alongside college courses, CTE, and associate degree programs.
chapters.title: Inzerillo commits to marking civics programs at District 26 high school fair

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: Chair Joseph, that's a great idea.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: We have a District 26 high school fair coming up on November 9th.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: And not only do we share with families high schools that provide college courses, CTE programs, associates degree programs.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: College now, early college.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: Yes, it's such a great idea.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: I will make sure that those high schools that

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: do come, that we have some kind of a marker or asterisk or some designation so families are well aware that they have an incredible civics program at those high schools as well.

chapters.summary: Joseph says information should go out through texts, websites, principals, parent coordinators, and SLTs. She says principals and parent coordinators are the first line of contact with families.
chapters.title: Joseph urges outreach through principals and parent coordinators

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yeah, correct.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So that's one way to get the information out, your text messages, your websites, and talking to your principals, right?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: They are the first line of defense who sees parents and families on it.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And engage your parent coordinators as well.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: They are also one of the folks that talk to parents and families and hold community meetings and get the word in the SLT as well.

chapters.summary: Inzerillo describes students researching a cannabis dispensary near a school and fixing water fountains at PS 173. He says students contact city agencies and hold officials accountable.
chapters.title: Inzerillo shares student civic action examples

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: We get the word out community as well.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: We had a elementary school student that was very concerned about some of the cannabis dispensaries.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: There was one that was relatively close within the 500 foot.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: And the student discovered it depends on how you measure those 500 feet.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: That student not only researched it.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: But they were so politically astute where they reached out to NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: They reached out to some of the local elected, reached out to my office.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: There were over 200 people that were at that cannabis dispensary just to learn more about like, hey, what's going on over here?

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: We share that same concern.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: So it is spreading.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: It is reaching.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: We had another student at PS 173 where the water fountains weren't working.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: So they reached out to the New York City Parks Commissioner, sent them a letter.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: And the New York City Parks Commissioner contacted me, the principal, and the student to say, not only do we fix it, but I would love for you and your class.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: meets to just check on it and make sure that it is working.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: So when we talk about partnerships, we have our students that reach out to the New York City Parks Department, Sanitation Department, the Building Department, all other departments within

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: New York City so that they can learn more about that and continue to create those partnerships, ask those great questions, and hold us all accountable.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: When I do principal performance observations, the principals will now

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: Warn me.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: I love it, though.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: They'll say, I want to let you know, Anthony, we have this civics group or the student organization group that are going to have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: So I think that is awesome.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: Thank you to all of you for supporting that.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: I know that you visit the schools and you get peppered by questions with students, but you're sharing the democratic process, ways in which students can get engaged.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: So thank you so much for that.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: We greatly appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks Inzerillo to confirm he will mark high schools that offer the Seal at the District 26 fair. Inzerillo says yes, the fair will distinguish civics, associate programs, college credit, and CTE.
chapters.title: Dinowitz confirms marker for Seal at high school fair

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure I heard you said that at the high schools, putting a little star or asterisk at the ones that do the CLA Civic Readiness.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: At the District 26 High School Fair, Chair Joseph gave me a great idea that we should have some kind of a marker for that.

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: So when we do have that high school fair on November 9th, we're going to make sure that we have some kind of a marker so families can see and distinguish

utterances.speaker: Anthony Inzerillo
utterances.text: what different high schools can offer, whether it's civics or associates program, college credit, CTE, and some of the other awesome and incredible programs that our high schools.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says the marker should also include the Seal of Biliteracy. He says the website needs an education component explaining what the Seal is so families understand the programs.
chapters.title: Dinowitz adds biliteracy and website education component

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, and I would just add, not to digress too much, but add the biliteracy.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Add the biliteracy there.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And to repeat, get it added to the website because these are things families search for, not just whether it has it, but what it is because there's also an education component that needs to go in.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like what is a seal of civic readiness that I think all the families deserve to know the schools they're going into have these really incredible programs that are rigorous, that are going to be looked at by CUNY for awarding college credit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And again, I'm looking forward to hearing about that meeting to really get into this so that...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Our high school students who do this work can get the college credit and more and more schools will be incentivized to offer this program.

chapters.summary: Joseph says young people see career pathways through civic engagement and thanks the agencies. She says she wants CUNY and DOE to be besties on civics, and Dinowitz jokes about karaoke after their meeting.
chapters.title: Joseph and Dinowitz close agency testimony with thanks and light remarks

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And young people see career pathways, right?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That's also career pathways.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So not only are they engaged, but they can see how can I make a difference in my community?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I think this is what the message is.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And thank you for doing that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: They hold us accountable, and I like that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph

chapters.summary: Elizabeth Shattuck leads social studies curriculum at New Visions for Public Schools and says the organization supports expanding Seal access. She offers instructional materials and professional learning, and recommends more approved project structures and rubrics.
chapters.title: Elizabeth Shattuck of New Visions testifies on Seal implementation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: My name is Elizabeth Shattuck, and I lead the social studies curriculum and professional learning team at New Visions for Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: New Visions has partnered with the city for 37 years on systems level change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: As an affinity partner, we support the leadership of a 71 school district, 71 school district, and we serve schools citywide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: New Visions for Public Schools strongly supports efforts to make the seal of civic readiness accessible and attainable in as many schools as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: We have worked with the Seal of Civic Readiness since 2018.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: After serving on New York State's Civic Education and Equity Task Force, we built tools to help schools implement the SEAL.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: And in the 21-22 school year, we piloted the SEAL in a small set of schools in partnership with Civics for All and Generation Citizen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: We expanded that work in the subsequent two years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: We support the effort by Education Chair...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: Genowitz, to expand access to the SEAL and to hands-on project-based civic education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: Further, we stand ready to partner with New York City Public Schools to develop and provide the high-quality instructional materials and professional learning needed to make meaningful student-led civics education a reality in grades 9 through 12.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: Many social studies teachers across New York State know new visions for public schools because of our free global history and U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: History curricula.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: They are among the most widely used in the city and the state, and they foreground primary source analysis, instructional routines in disciplinary literacy, and discourse skills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: Our experience developing these materials in partnership with teachers and conducting professional learning to support effective materials use

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: has given us insight into what it will take to ensure the seal of civic readiness can reach all high schools in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: First, throughout our work on the SEAL and Civics of Education, teachers have told us what would help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: A project structure and rubrics already approved for SEAL credit, which they could build a course around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: The Civics for All citywide approved list is the right mechanism, and there should be more materials made available through this process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: Second, teachers appreciate high-quality, engaging professional learning that supports their

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: ability to implement instructional materials well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: We have found that workshops grounded in specific instructional materials provide the specific support that many teachers need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: This is even more important now, as teachers are trying to learn not only about instruction, but evaluating student work in an era where students have access to AI outside school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: Finally, as many other civics education organizations have pointed out, the learning that goes into civics projects has to start as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: In the New Vision Social Studies course sequence, civic starts in ninth grade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: Our materials use ancient history to struggle with the same civic questions as the very first civilizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: Who holds power?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: How do resources get divided?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: And whose interest does a system serve?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: Students then apply those questions to their own communities using structured project opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elizabeth Shattuck
utterances.text: New Visions applauds Council Member Denowitz and the New York City Council for taking on this important effort, and we look forward to engaging in continued support of civic readiness for all New York City students.

utterances.text: And I just hope that they can receive credit accordingly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public

chapters.summary: Jeffrey Rehm, executive director of Runway Green, describes a planned education campus at Floyd Bennett Field serving up to 50,000 students yearly. He urges the Council to adopt all three resolutions and support educator preparation and community partnerships.
chapters.title: Jeffrey Rehm of Runway Green testifies on civic learning at Floyd Bennett Field

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: Hi, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs and committee members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: I'm Jeffrey Rehm, executive director of Runway Green, a Brooklyn nonprofit expanding real-world learning for New York City students, proud former public school teacher and leader of a couple of New York City outward-bound schools, which have gotten some shout-outs today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: At a time of deep division and uncertainty, young people need opportunities to examine evidence, engage across differences, and see that their participation matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: We strongly support these resolutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: And through New York Inspires and the Portrait of a Graduate, New York is now reconsidering what counts as learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: How students demonstrate it, and what a diploma signifies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reinvest in education's purpose, which is to build a better world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: When done well, the Seal of Civic Readiness puts this purpose into practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: Strong implementation, broad access, and college credit could make it a model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: For the learning that New York inspires is meant to bring to life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: Runway Green is working toward that vision with a signed 60-year National Park Service lease.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: We're developing an education campus at Floyd Bennett Field that could serve up to 50,000 students every single year from New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: Student pilots are underway with programs in development with New York City Public Schools, with CUNY, and with community partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: I want to paint a picture of what this might look like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: Imagine students along the shores of Jamaica Bay, wind pulling at their jackets as they investigate coastal flooding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: They collect water level data, hear residents'accounts of storms, weigh policy options, and present recommendations to local decision makers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: This work connects classroom learning to public problems, shows students their power to influence their communities, and creates opportunities for high school and college credit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: We urge the council to adopt all three resolutions and support educator preparation and community partnership aligned with New York Inspires so students across the city can participate in rigorous civic learning and receive meaningful recognition for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Rehm
utterances.text: Appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I don't want to take long, but before I go, I'll stay here to listen because this is such a great, awesome plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We've been going through it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: So I want to say publicly, I am so thankful for you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And I know why we become besties, because of our children, the future agriculture environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And it's such a thing that we have to cross that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We have to walk that line, making sure that our children have a better tomorrow and understand what is environment like and what is agriculture like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: And thank you for your leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I just want to say thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susie Gomes
utterances.text: When my children were in preschool, I began teaching them to solve for X.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susie Gomes
utterances.text: The point, besides me being a math geek, is that math is everywhere in our life, and math is a block of concepts that build on each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susie Gomes
utterances.text: The same applies to civics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susie Gomes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairpersons Joseph and Dinoids and members of the New York City Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: Council's Committees on Higher Education and Education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: My name is Davia Willis, Chairperson-Elect of the CUNY University Student Senate for the 2026-2027 academic year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: I am honored to testify today regarding the Seal of Civic Readiness, Academic Credit Recognition, and the expansion of civic education opportunities for New York City students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: The CUNY University Student Senate believes there is tremendous value in exposing students to civic education and engagement early in their academic journeys.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: When students are introduced to how the government works, the legislative process, and the importance of community involvement, they are not simply learning about democracy, they are developing the knowledge and confidence to actively participate in it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: As a graduate student from CUNY John Jay College, I have witnessed firsthand the benefits of civic engagement through my experience with the CUNY University Student Senate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: Over the years, our organization has gained significant momentum because of students who have brought their leadership experiences, community involvement, and passion for advocacy to the work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: Into the work that we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: A clear example is the CUNY University Student Senate Omnicard campaign, where student advocacy and engagement with elected officials helped secure $700,000 from the New York City Council toward a student omnicard program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: This achievement demonstrated what students can accomplish when they understand the legislative process and recognize that their voices have the power to influence

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: public policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: This is why we also support the Next Gen Civics Act, which would introduce more hands-on project-based education, civic education in high schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: We believe students should have the opportunities to apply what they learn rather than simply reading about government and civic responsibility in the textbooks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: Furthermore, the CUNY University Student Senate agrees that students who have already demonstrated civic competencies and earned the seal of civic readiness should enter college knowing that their work has academic value.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: We also recognize that CUNY has established pathways for awarding credit for prior learning and that civic readiness can be demonstrated through different experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: Therefore, the consideration of what constitutes appropriate college credit must account for these differences while ensuring that students are evaluated fairly and consistently against established academic standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: As CUNY continues to explore these pathways, I would encourage the university to ensure that any credits awarded meaningfully

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: Any credits awarded meaningfully contribute towards students'degree requirements, potentially reducing their financial burden and bringing them closer to graduation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: The CUNY University Student Senate equally supports expanding access to SEAL across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: Access to the seal across New York City public high schools because opportunities for civic education and recognition should not be determined by which school a student attends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: Civic education should not simply prepare students to understand democracy, but empower them to participate in it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: As we recognize the work students have already accomplished, we must also continue creating opportunities for them to become the leaders and advocates of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Davia Willis
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and consideration.

chapters.summary: Hazel Praise Aqua, a Lehman College political science graduate from Ghana, says she had to relearn how government works in the U.S. She supports Res 620, Res 451, and Res 418 so all students can access civic education and recognition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Joseph and, you know, its end members.

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Joseph and Dinowitz and members of the New York City Council's Committees on Higher Education and Education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: I'm a political science graduate of Lehman College, a student advocate here on behalf of the CUNY University Student Senate, and someone...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: Who believes that civic education should be an opportunity available to every student, not just a select few.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: When I moved to the United States from Ghana, I realized that understanding government was not something I could take for granted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: I had to relearn how the government worked here, how policies were made, how to navigate civic institutions, and how to understand my rights and responsibilities in a new system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: That experience taught me something important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: We cannot expect young people to participate in a system they have not been given the tools to understand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: My journey studying political science and serving in student government, the CUNY University Student Senate, and other student leadership roles has showed me the power of civic education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: When students understand how decisions are made,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: They begin to recognize that their voices matter and that they have the power to influence change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: That is why I support the expansion of the New York State Seal of Civic Readiness across New York City public high schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: Resolution 0620 is an important step toward ensuring that every eligible student has the opportunity to learn this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: recognition, regardless of which public

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: high school they attend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: Access to civic education and recognition of civic achievement should not depend on a student's zip code or school resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: I also support Resolution 0451 and the Next Gen Civics Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: Students need more than textbooks and lectures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: They need hands-on experiences that teach them how to engage with their communities, understand public policy, advocate for themselves, and turn their ideas into meaningful action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: Finally, Resolution 0401A addresses an important next step, ensuring that students who end the SEAL receive appropriate

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: College Credit at CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: If we tell students that civic engagement matters, we must recognize the work that they have already done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: Their learning, leadership, and service should have value as they transition into higher education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: Civic education should not end at graduation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: It should create a pathway from the classroom to college, from college to community leadership, and from community leadership to lasting change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: I stand here today as someone who had to learn a new system, find my voice within it, and discover the power of participation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: I want every student, whether they were born here or came from somewhere else, to have that same opportunity without unnecessary barriers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: Our young people are not simply future leaders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: They are members of our communities right now, and they deserve the knowledge, resources, and recognition to help them shape their future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and consideration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ashley Pagaro

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ashley Pagaro

chapters.summary: Alan Sherman, a NYC resident since 1961, says respect for people who think differently is disappearing from political culture. He urges civics education that teaches independent thinking, respectful debate, and compromise.
chapters.title: Alan Sherman testifies on independent thinking and civic respect

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Okay, now it's time for something different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: My name is Alan Sherman, and I have been a New York City resident since 1961.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: I have always had a strong interest in government and politics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: When people have asked me to run for office, I respond by always saying I run from office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Over the years, I have witnessed many changes in our society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: One thing I have always valued is respect for people who think differently from us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that respect seems to be disappearing from our political culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Recently, I have become involved with various political campaigns, both Democrat and Republican.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: In my view, it should not matter which party you're part of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Too often, both parties have become more concerned with partisan politics than with working together to solve problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: I encourage people to look beyond party labels and evaluate candidates based on who they are, what they stand for, and whether their proposals reflect their own beliefs and values.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: I have registered many people to vote over the past few years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: I have discovered that many recently do not know how to research candidates or evaluate their positions on important issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: I try to teach them that their responsibility does not end with registering to vote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: They must also take the time to learn about the candidates on both sides of issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: And make informed decisions based on their own convictions, not simply their political party affiliation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: This is where civic education becomes so important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Our school system must do a better job of teaching students how our government works, how elections function, and what it means to be an informed and responsible citizen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Students should understand that they do not have to vote for every candidate from the same political party.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: They can vote for a Democrat in one race and Republican in another race.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Neither party has all the answers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Neither party is automatically right or wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Our future is at risk if we allow our children to grow up believing that one political side is always good and the other is always bad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Patients should encourage independent thinking, not indoctrination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Students must learn to research issues, examine different perspectives, and ask questions and reach their own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: We are all human beings, and most of us want what is best for our communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: We need to teach young people not only how the government operates, but also the role that they play in making it work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Civics education, along with practical knowledge about everyday life, is essential to maintaining a healthy, informed, and vibrant society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Educators have a responsibility to prevent different viewpoints fairly and encourage students to think critically.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Our classrooms should be places where students learn how to think, not what to think.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: They should be equipped to examine political arguments independently and make up their own minds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Finally, I believe the simplest and most effective way to improve our political climate is also one that most overlook, sitting down over a cup of coffee with someone you disagree with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: I have found that these conversations can lower the temperature, build mutual respect, and open the door to compromise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: We do not have to agree on everything to listen to one another or treat each other with dignity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: I urge the council to support a civic education curriculum that teaches independent

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: independent thinking, political awareness, respectful debate, and the value of compromise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: If we want a stronger democracy, we must teach the next generation how to participate in it responsibly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: That begins with education, open-mindedness, and willingness to listen, even when we disagree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alan Sherman
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and consideration.

chapters.summary: Hazel Praise Aqua says she learned Ghanaian civic education from grade one to grade nine. She says U.S. students often lack historical and political context, leaving professors to teach basics in college.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: So with what he said, like people not being educated, I really agree with that because I grew up in Ghana.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: But then when I came here as a political science student, I tried to have these conversations with other people and they don't even know what America's history is or the whole political context about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: And that really confused me because I'm like, didn't they teach you guys anything at all?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: But then they are now learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
utterances.text: And it makes things hard for our professors, too, because they talk about stuff expecting the students that are from here to know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hazel Praise Aqua
